title: If You Started College in 1966, This Was Your Life

scenes.text: It's a hot day in early September of nineteen sixty-six. Your father pulls the family car up in front of a brick dormitory. In the trunk, there's a suitcase, a typewriter, a clock radio, a reading lamp and a box of sheets your mother ironed. You're eighteen years old. And you're about to become the first person in your family to go to college.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER, 1966

scenes.text: Millions of young Americans made that same trip in the sixties. In nineteen sixty, about three and a half million Americans were enrolled in college. By nineteen seventy, it was more than eight million. Colleges were building new dorms, new classrooms and whole new campuses as fast as they could.
scenes.caption: 8 MILLION STUDENTS

scenes.text: And if you started college in the fall of sixty-six, you were about to live through four of the most dramatic years in American history. Let's follow a freshman from that first day on campus to graduation in nineteen seventy.
scenes.caption: FOUR DRAMATIC YEARS

scenes.text: Before you even arrived, there was the acceptance letter. It came in the mail, in a thick envelope if the news was good, and a thin one if it wasn't. Most students applied to only one or two schools, often the state university or a college close to home. And many chose their school simply because a parent, a teacher or an older cousin had gone there.
scenes.caption: THE THICK ENVELOPE

scenes.text: College in nineteen sixty-six had a lot of rules, especially for women. Most campuses were still run on a principle called in loco parentis, which meant the college acted in place of your parents. Women's dorms had curfews, often ten or eleven o'clock on weeknights. A housemother at the front desk checked everyone in.
scenes.caption: IN LOCO PARENTIS

scenes.text: Men were not allowed in women's dorms, except in the lobby, during visiting hours. On some campuses, if a man visited a woman's room on a special open house day, the door had to stay open, and everyone had to keep at least one foot on the floor. Women who came in late could be punished, or even sent home.
scenes.caption: ONE FOOT ON THE FLOOR

scenes.text: Many schools still had dress codes. Women wore skirts to class and to dinner. Men wore slacks and collared shirts, and sometimes a jacket and tie in the dining hall. At some schools, freshmen even had to wear little caps, called beanies, during their first weeks, so upperclassmen could pick them out.
scenes.caption: THE FRESHMAN BEANIE

scenes.text: Meals were served in a big dining hall, cafeteria style, at set times. Miss dinner and you went hungry, or walked to the snack bar for a grilled cheese. The food was famously bad. Mystery meat, soggy vegetables and Jell-O in every color. Students complained endlessly, and then went back for seconds.
scenes.caption: MYSTERY MEAT

scenes.text: What did college cost? In nineteen sixty-six, the average yearly tuition at a public four-year college was only a few hundred dollars. Room and board added maybe seven or eight hundred more. A whole year at a state university could cost around twelve hundred dollars. At a private college, it might be twice that.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $1,200 A YEAR

scenes.text: That sounds incredible today, but the minimum wage in nineteen sixty-six was a dollar twenty-five an hour. Even so, many students paid their own way with a summer job, working in a factory, at a resort or on a road crew. They graduated with little or no debt. Today, the average yearly cost at a public university is many times higher, even after inflation.
scenes.caption: A SUMMER JOB PAID FOR IT

scenes.text: And for many, college was paid for by the government. The Higher Education Act of nineteen sixty-five created new grants and student loans for families who couldn't afford college. For the first time, millions of working-class kids, the sons and daughters of factory workers and farmers, could go.
scenes.caption: THE HIGHER EDUCATION ACT

scenes.text: Dorm rooms were small and simple. Two metal beds, two desks, two dressers and a sink in the corner, if you were lucky. Your roommate was a stranger, picked by the college, and you met for the first time on move-in day. Some roommates became lifelong friends. Others barely lasted a week.
scenes.caption: YOUR ROOMMATE

scenes.text: There was one telephone on each floor, a pay phone in the hallway. When it rang, whoever was closest answered and shouted down the hall. Long distance calls home were expensive, so students called once a week, usually on Sunday night, when rates were cheaper. Parents waited by the phone.
scenes.caption: ONE PHONE PER FLOOR

scenes.text: Most of the communication was by letter. Students wrote home every week, often asking for money. Parents sent back letters with a check, a few dollars in cash, or a care package of homemade cookies. Getting mail was the highlight of the day. An empty mailbox could ruin a whole afternoon.
scenes.caption: LETTERS HOME

scenes.text: And there was laundry. For many young men, college was the first time they had ever washed their own clothes. Some mailed their laundry home in a special canvas case, and their mothers mailed it back clean and folded, sometimes with cookies tucked inside. Others just let it pile up until it couldn't be ignored.
scenes.caption: MAILING THE LAUNDRY HOME

scenes.text: Classes were big. Freshman lectures might have several hundred students in a huge hall, with a professor at the front and a microphone. Students took notes by hand, in spiral notebooks. Papers were typed on a manual or electric typewriter, with carbon paper for a copy. A typing mistake meant correction fluid, or starting the page over.
scenes.caption: THE LECTURE HALL

scenes.text: The library was the center of the academic world. No internet, no computers. Students searched the card catalog, a huge wooden cabinet full of little drawers, and then hunted for books in the stacks. Research for a term paper could take weeks. During finals, the library stayed open late, and every chair was full.
scenes.caption: THE CARD CATALOG

scenes.text: Calculations were done with a slide rule, a ruler with a sliding middle piece. Engineering students carried them in a leather case on their belts. Electronic calculators wouldn't be affordable until the seventies. Computers existed, but they filled entire rooms, and students fed them programs on stacks of punched cards.
scenes.caption: THE SLIDE RULE

scenes.text: Grades mattered more than ever. A bad semester could mean losing a scholarship, or, for young men, losing a draft deferment. Students pulled all-nighters fueled by black coffee and No-Doz tablets. During exam week, the dorms went quiet. And when grades were posted on a bulletin board in the hallway, crowds gathered to look for their student numbers.
scenes.caption: THE ALL-NIGHTER

scenes.text: Social life revolved around the weekend. Fraternities and sororities were at the height of their popularity. Rush week came every fall. There were mixers, where boys from one dorm met girls from another, with a band or a record player and punch in a bowl. Homecoming was a huge event, with a parade, floats and a football game.
scenes.caption: HOMECOMING

scenes.text: On Saturday afternoons, the whole campus went to the football game. Students wore their school colors, cheered with the band, and carried pennants. In winter, it was basketball. Afterward, there were parties, dances and late-night trips to the diner for burgers and fries.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY AFTERNOON

scenes.text: And there was the music. In nineteen sixty-six and sixty-seven, college students listened to the Beatles' Revolver and Sgt. Pepper's, Bob Dylan, Simon and Garfunkel, the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds, and the Doors. Every dorm room had a record player. And late at night, students listened to new FM radio stations that played whole album sides.
scenes.caption: SGT. PEPPER'S

scenes.text: Dating had its own rituals. A man asked a woman out days in advance, by phone or in person. He picked her up at the dorm lobby, signed her out with the housemother, and had her back before curfew. If they got serious, he gave her his fraternity pin, which was called getting pinned. It was the step before engagement, and many couples married right after graduation.
scenes.caption: GETTING PINNED

scenes.text: For young men in college in the late sixties, there was one thing always in the back of their minds. The draft. The war in Vietnam was growing. In nineteen sixty-six, the United States had about three hundred eighty thousand troops there, and the number kept rising. Every month, thousands of young men were drafted.
scenes.caption: THE DRAFT

scenes.text: College students could get a student deferment, called a two-S, which postponed the draft while they were in school. But they had to stay enrolled and keep their grades up. Some men stayed in school, or went on to graduate school, partly to avoid being sent to Vietnam. Flunking out could mean a ticket to the jungle.
scenes.caption: THE 2-S DEFERMENT

scenes.text: In December of nineteen sixty-nine, the government held the first draft lottery since World War Two. Every birthday was drawn, one by one, on live television. Young men gathered in dorm lounges to watch. If your birthday came up with a low number, you were likely to be drafted. If it was high, you were probably safe. It was one of the most tense nights of their lives.
scenes.caption: THE DRAFT LOTTERY

scenes.text: By nineteen sixty-seven and sixty-eight, campuses were changing fast. Students protested the war, marched for civil rights, and demanded a voice in how their colleges were run. Teach-ins, rallies and sit-ins became common. Some students joined the protests. Many more simply watched, studied and worried.
scenes.caption: THE PROTESTS

scenes.text: Styles changed too. Freshmen who arrived in sixty-six with crew cuts and pleated skirts looked very different by seventy. Hair got longer. Skirts got shorter, then much longer. Jeans and sandals replaced slacks and loafers. And one by one, the old rules about curfews and dress codes disappeared.
scenes.caption: STYLES CHANGED

scenes.text: Nineteen sixty-eight was the hardest year. In April, Martin Luther King Junior was killed. In June, Robert Kennedy was killed. Students who had grown up believing in a bright future suddenly saw a country in turmoil. Many say that year changed them more than any class they ever took.

In July of nineteen sixty-nine, many students were home for the summer when Apollo eleven landed on the moon. They watched it on the family television, with their parents and little brothers and sisters. After everything that had happened, it was a moment of pure pride. For one night, the whole country seemed to be cheering together.
scenes.caption: JULY 1969

scenes.text: And then, in the spring of nineteen seventy, the class that started in sixty-six graduated. They had arrived in a world of beanies and curfews and left in a world that had been turned upside down. That May, the shootings at Kent State in Ohio shook campuses across the country. Some schools canceled classes and even graduation ceremonies.
scenes.caption: THE CLASS OF 1970

scenes.text: But most of them walked across the stage, shook the president's hand, and took their diploma, while their parents cried in the audience. For many, they were the first in their family ever to graduate from college. It was the proudest day of their parents' lives.
scenes.caption: THE PROUDEST DAY

scenes.text: The class of nineteen seventy went on to become teachers, engineers, lawyers, nurses, business owners and soldiers. They raised families, built careers and lived through everything that came next. But many say those four years, from sixty-six to seventy, shaped who they were for the rest of their lives.
scenes.caption: SHAPED FOR LIFE

scenes.text: Today, college looks very different. No curfews. No beanies. Computers in every pocket. But it costs far more, and many students graduate with tens of thousands of dollars in debt. In nineteen sixty-six, a young person could pay for college with a summer job. That's almost impossible today.
scenes.caption: THEN AND NOW

scenes.text: If you started college in the late sixties, you remember it. The typewriter in your dorm room. The pay phone in the hall. The letters from home with a five-dollar bill inside. The roommate you'll never forget. And the feeling that the whole world was changing, and you were right in the middle of it.
scenes.caption: YOU WERE RIGHT IN THE MIDDLE

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Where did you go to college, and what year did you start? What was your dorm like, and what do you remember most? We read every comment. Next time, we're looking at the truth about the nineteen sixties kitchen your mother trusted. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHERE DID YOU GO TO COLLEGE?
